paper_title: No Channels Left Behind: Understanding Diffusion Acceleration through Residual Gates

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Training acceleration methods for diffusion transformers, such as REPA and dispersive regularization, are commonly explained by additional supervision, spatial-structure priors, or improved feature geometry. We revisit this view and uncover a striking internal change: the AdaLN-Zero residual gate $α$, which directly controls how conditioned updates enter the residual stream, is substantially reorganized by these methods. This observation motivates our hypothesis that acceleration arises, at least in part, from reshaping the residual gating pathway rather than solely from the feature structures explicitly imposed by auxiliary objectives. Supporting this view, accelerated models are markedly more sensitive to perturbations of $α$, and their gate geometry reflects semantic relationships among classes. We further introduce the normalized participation ratio (nPR) to characterize the channel-wise organization of the gates and find that, across REPA teachers, projector architectures, and radial-objective targets, broader gate participation accompanies better generation quality. Guided by this insight, we propose a simple teacher-free radial objective that promotes broader gate participation through feature-norm regularization, without pairwise feature comparisons. On ImageNet $256\times256$ with SiT-B/2, our method improves FID over dispersive loss while increasing mean gate participation over timesteps and classes, further supporting the link between gate organization and training acceleration. Our results identify residual-gate reorganization as a measurable axis of diffusion training acceleration and suggest a simple direction for further acceleration.

sections.title: ABSTRACT
sections.content: Training acceleration methods for diffusion transformers, such as REPA and dispersive regularization, are commonly explained by additional supervision, spatialstructure priors, or improved feature geometry. This observation motivates our hypothesis that acceleration arises, at least in part, from reshaping the residual gating pathway rather than solely from the feature structures explicitly imposed by auxiliary objectives. Supporting this view, accelerated models are markedly more sensitive to perturbations of α, and their gate geometry reflects semantic relationships among classes. We further introduce the normalized participation ratio (nPR) to characterize the channel-wise organization of the gates and find that, across REPA teachers, projector architectures, and radial-objective targets, broader gate participation accompanies better generation quality. Guided by this insight, we propose simple teacher-free radial objective that promotes broader gate participation through feature-norm regularization, without pairwise feature comparisons. Our results identify residual-gate reorganization as measurable axis of diffusion training acceleration and suggest simple direction for further acceleration. Our code is available at https://github.com/naver-ai/radialobj

sections.title: INTRODUCTION
sections.content: Recent advances have substantially accelerated diffusion transformer training by injecting additional auxiliary objectives through representation alignment (REPA) with frozen-teacher supervision (Yu et al., 2025), spatially structured representation alignment (Singh et al., 2026), and feature-geometry regularization (Wang & He, 2025). Despite their differences, these approaches are largely understood through the representational structures explicitly imposed by their objectives. Yet, are these structures themselves responsible for faster training, or do they reshape more fundamental mechanism within the transformer? We revisit this question through the conditioning pathway of AdaLN-Zero (Peebles & Xie, 2023). In diffusion transformers such as DiT (Peebles & Xie, 2023) and SiT (Ma et al., 2024), timestep and class embeddings generate modulation vectors for every transformer block. Among them, the residual gate α1 plays particularly direct role: it scales each channel of branch output before residual addition, thus controlling how strongly each feature channel contributes to the residual stream across all token positions. This suggests complementary view of diffusion acceleration: auxiliary objectives may not only reshape the features they supervise, but also reorganize how those features are injected into the residual stream. We therefore conjecture that residual gating may provide common internal signature of accelerated diffusion training  (Fig. 1)  . To this end, we begin with two simple interventions: removing the AdaLN-Zero modulation pathway during training and perturbing the residual gate itself at test time. Gating matters even for the Done during internship at NAVER AI Lab. 1We refer to α as gate, as it modulates the embeddings through channel-wise multiplication.

sections.title: Preprint
sections.content: Figure 1: Overview: from residual gate insights to improved diffusion training. (Left) AdaLNZero gates scale residual-branch outputs channel-wise, with each gate shared across token positions. (Center) Our proposed normalized participation ratio (nPR) measures how evenly squared gate magnitudes are distributed across channels. Across REPA teachers, higher mean gate participation is associated with lower FID. (Right) Our proposed Radial objective penalizes per-sample feature norms without pretrained teacher or pairwise feature comparisons. baseline (without acceleration), but strikingly, accelerated models are far more vulnerable to its disruption. This contrast suggests that acceleration does more than improve the features being learned: it fundamentally changes how the model uses them through the gating pathway. Motivated by this observation, we first ask whether residual gates carry interpretable semantic structure. Using WordNet (Fellbaum, 1998), we find that distances between class-conditioned gates increase with semantic distance between classes, indicating that the gating pathway reflects the semantic organization of the generated categories. Next, we quantify gate participation using the normalized participation ratio (nPR), scale-invariant measure of how broadly gate magnitude is distributed across channels that also guides our subsequent method design. Higher gate participation, averaged over timesteps and classes, tracks better generation quality across REPA teachers and, for fixed teacher, across projector designs, identifying gate participation as correlate of generation quality within each sweep. Based on gate participation, we introduce the Radial objective, simple teacher-free objective that acts only on hidden-feature norms. Unlike representation alignment, it requires no pretrained teacher guidance; unlike dispersive regularization, it requires no pairwise feature comparisons. Instead, the Radial objective penalizes deviations of each samples flattened feature norm from target. Despite acting only on feature norms, this objective increases residual-gate participation and improves generation quality. As result, our method improves both Frechet inception distance (FID; Heusel et al., 2017) and mean gate participation, supporting residual-gate participation as candidate mechanism underlying diffusion training acceleration. Quantitatively, on ImageNet 256256 (Deng et al., 2009) with SiT-B/2 trained for 400K steps, the Radial objective achieves an FID of 11.83, improving over Vanilla2 (16.24) and Dispersive (13.19), while increasing the mean final-block MLP gate participation from 0.434 in Vanilla to 0.642. Overall, our results point beyond the representations explicitly targeted by existing acceleration methods. These objectives also reorganize the residual gating pathway, whose channel participation tracks generation quality in controlled sweeps. We argue that this perspective identifies residual-gate organization as previously overlooked axis of diffusion acceleration and provides simple route to promote it without either representation teacher or pairwise feature comparisons.

sections.content: Diffusion transformers process latent image tokens through transformer blocks containing multihead self-attention (MHSA) branch and an MLP branch (Peebles & Xie, 2023). Each branch adds an update to the residual stream. We study the AdaLN-Zero conditioning used in these blocks. Let RN denote tokens with channels. Here, γ and β specify the scale and shift of the normalized branch input; α scales the branch output before residual addition. Accordingly, α may be interpreted as residual gating vector. The Hadamard product acts channel-wise, with each vector broadcast across tokens; MHSA and MLP branches have separate modulation parameters in each block. Note that α is structurally distinct: Whereas β and γ modulate the branch input and are mediated by the subsequent projection layers in MHSA or MLP, α directly gates the branch output before residual addition. We thus conjecture that training acceleration is governed primarily by α. We refer to α as the channel-wise residual gate: αd multiplies channel at every token position. Its entries are signed scaling coefficients. The gate is obtained directly from the conditioning pathway, without an image forward pass. Because α directly scales the residual branch output, it lets us examine how conditioning controls each channels contribution to the residual stream. We first test how generation quality responds to changes in the gates channel-wise magnitude distribution, then examine the structure of gates learned under accelerated training. Prior work has examined AdaLN initialization and parameter updates (Zhu et al., 2026) and the semantic structure of conditioning embeddings (Pham et al., 2026). How the residual gate values organize channel contributions under accelerated training remains underexplored. Diffusion transformer acceleration and its mechanics. Recent auxiliary losses to accelerate diffusion transformer training fall into two broad categories: teacher-guided (REPA (Yu et al., 2025) and iREPA (Singh et al., 2026)) and teacher-free (dispersive loss (Wang & He, 2025)). REPA and iREPA accelerate training by aligning diffusion features with representations from frozen vision foundation model through learnable projector. Dispersive loss is regularizer that encourages larger pairwise ℓ2 distances between the hidden features of samples within batch.

sections.title: 3 UNDERSTANDING ACCELERATION IN DIFFUSION TRANSFORMERS
sections.content: 3.1 MOTIVATION What lies beyond existing representation-level supervision? Existing explanations for diffusion acceleration largely focus on the representations explicitly targeted by the auxiliary objective: REPA guides hidden features toward pretrained visual representations (Yu et al., 2025), while dispersive objectives reshape their geometry (Wang & He, 2025). We conjecture that these feature-level effects are not the full story. Instead, acceleration may critically depend on how such supervision reorganizes the AdaLN-Zero gating pathway (beyond prior initialization analyses (Zhu et al., 2026)), which directly controls the contribution of conditioned residual updates throughout the network. Pilot study 1: How does gating affect generation quality during training? We perform pilot study by training models with in-context conditioning (Peebles & Xie, 2023) in place of AdaLNZero, removing its conditional modulation pathway, including the residual gate. The FID improvements from both Dispersive and REPA become substantially smaller under in-context conditioning  (Table 1)  . Relative to Vanilla, REPAs FID change shifts from 18.24 to 13.48, while Dispersives shifts from 4.98 to +1.15. This comparison supports role for the AdaLN-Zero modulation pathway in the gains from auxiliary objectives; Pilot 2 isolates the residual gate. sections.title: INCREASING GATE PARTICIPATION FOR BETTER GENERATION QUALITY
sections.content: This section studies whether encouraging higher gate participation during training improves generation quality. We introduce the Radial objective, which acts on hidden-feature norms, and examine when its local gradient contribution increases gate participation.

sections.title: 5 DISCUSSION AND LIMITATIONS
sections.content: Interpreting iREPA and spatial structure. iREPA motivates its convolutional projector and spatial normalization as ways to improve the transfer of spatial structure from teacher representations (Singh et al., 2026). Its spatial diagnostics, including LDS, summarize how similarity between patch tokens varies with their spatial separation. Our fixed-teacher projector sweep in Section 3.2.2 helps distinguish properties that change together when replacing an MLP with convolution: nonlinear depth, channel transformation, and spatial mixing. At 50K steps, the 1 1 projector reaches FID 51.33, compared with 51.68 for an additional 3 3 convolutional projector trained under the same teacher normalization and alignment settings. The comparable quality of these two heads shows that

sections.title: Preprint
sections.content: neighboring-token mixing inside the projector is not required to attain this performance in the tested configuration. The lower FID of the deep linear head relative to the nonlinear MLP also motivates examining the effect of projector nonlinearities. Association and intervention. The teacher and projector sweeps show recurring relationship between gate participation and FID within their respective experimental settings. The post-hoc pilot establishes sensitivity to gate modification, but its uniformizing interventions do not consistently improve generation quality. The WordNet analysis shows class-related structure in the gates; it does not establish lower bound on the participation needed to represent semantic hierarchy. The Radial objective provides simple teacher-free training objective that yields higher participation and lower FID in the tested target sweep. It acts on feature norms and affects the gates indirectly, alongside other model parameters. The local gradient proposition specifies conditions for positive radial contribution (Appendix D.1); it does not guarantee participation growth under the full optimizer or establish that such growth causes the FID improvement.

sections.title: 6 RELATED WORK
sections.content: Representation alignment in diffusion transformers. REPA supervises intermediate diffusion features with pretrained visual representations, motivated by the difficulty of learning useful representations from the generative objective alone (Yu et al., 2025). Subsequent work examines the alignment target and projector in iREPA (Singh et al., 2026), and the timing and scope of alignment in HASTE, which combines feature and attention-map supervision before terminating alignment during training (Wang et al., 2025). Our analysis concerns the internal modulation induced by these training choices, focusing on residual-gate participation and geometry. Spatial structure in diffusion representations. iREPA compares global semantic performance with spatial self-similarity in teacher representations and motivates changes intended to improve the transfer of spatial information (Singh et al., 2026). HASTE also incorporates spatial relationships through attention-map supervision (Wang et al., 2025). Our projector experiments instead examine the role of projection architecture within the tested alignment configurations, without making broader claim about the necessity of spatial information in diffusion models. Adaptive modulation and gating in DiTs. DiT uses adaptive normalization and residual scaling through AdaLN-Zero (Peebles & Xie, 2023); SiT adopts this transformer backbone for interpolantbased generative modeling (Ma et al., 2024). Related analyses examine modulation initialization (Zhu et al., 2026) and the concentration of semantic information in conditional embeddings (Pham et al., 2026). We focus specifically on the learned branch-specific residual gate α, its allocation across channels, and its geometry across training objectives. Representation geometry and effective dimensionality. Sparsity measures characterize the concentration of coefficients (Hurley & Rickard, 2008), while intrinsic-dimension estimates have been used to assess self-supervised representations (Mordacq et al., 2026). Dispersive training modifies representation geometry through an auxiliary separation objective (Wang & He, 2025). We apply participation ratio to squared gate coordinates in the models channel basis. This measures the allocation of gate magnitude across channels, rather than the spectral rank or intrinsic dimension of hidden representations, and serves here as diagnostic associated with generation quality.

sections.title: 7 CONCLUSION
sections.content: We examined diffusion transformer acceleration through class-conditioned residual gates. Accelerated models depend more strongly on these gates: removing the AdaLN-Zero modulation shrinks their gains, and perturbing α degrades REPA the most. The gates also reflect the semantic hierarchy among classes, most strongly under REPA, and their gate participation tracks FID across REPA teachers and, for fixed teacher, across projectors. Building on this, the teacher-free Radial objective raised gate participation and improved FID over Dispersive without pairwise feature comparisons. Because gate participation is computed from the conditioning pathway alone, without an image forward pass, it offers lightweight quantity to monitor in accelerated diffusion training.

sections.title: AI USE STATEMENT
sections.content: In this work, we used generative AI tools to write small pieces of code for implementing our methods, to assist in writing proofs, and to formulate mathematical claims. We have not used generative AI tools to develop theoretical models or conceptual frameworks, to provide critical ingredients for proofs, to propose or refine hypotheses, to design or give feedback on the research methodology or experiments, to interpret results, or to translate text. Synthetic data generation, dataset cleaning and reformatting, and qualitative or thematic data analysis are not applicable to this work. Additionally, we used generative AI tools to search for related work, to edit the paper for readability, and to check its formatting. We emphasize that generative AI did not originate the core methodology or generate the full experimental codebase. We have reviewed all AI-assisted work: the authors derived and verified all mathematical claims and proofs themselves, AI-assisted code was validated through sanity checks and by reproducing published baseline results, and every work found through AI-assisted search was checked against the original paper. We take responsibility for the final content of this work, including text, claims, code, analyses, and results produced with the aid of generative AI.

sections.title: A COMMON SETUP
sections.content: A.1 MODELS AND TRAINING All experiments use class-conditional ImageNet (Deng et al., 2009) generation at 256 256 resolution with SiT (Ma et al., 2024) and AdaLN-Zero, except the in-context conditioning ablation of Pilot study 1 (Appendix B.1). The teacher sweep, gate intervention, hierarchy analysis, and gate histograms use SiT-XL/2, with 28 blocks, hidden width 1,152, and 16 attention heads. The projector and Radial objective experiments use SiT-B/2, with 12 blocks, width 768, and 12 heads. Both architectures use 2 2 latent patches and an MLP expansion ratio of four. Layer numbers are one-based: L1 denotes the first transformer block. Local SiT-B/2 training. Unless stated otherwise, our SiT-B/2 runs use seed 42, global batch size 256, bfloat16 mixed precision, and AdamW (Loshchilov & Hutter, 2019) with constant learning rate of 104, β1 = 0.9, β2 = 0.999, and zero weight decay. The label-drop probability is 0.1 and the EMA decay is 0.9999. Our SiT-B/2 Dispersive runs use the best-performing PyTorch configuration of the official implementation (Wang & He, 2025): the InfoNCE-L2 dispersive loss on the finalblock output (L12) with coefficient λ = 0.25 and temperature τ = 1, computed within each perGPU batch of 32 on eight GPUs. The velocity objective uses linear interpolation path. Training uses cached ImageNet latents from the ft-MSE VAE, sampled from the stored posterior. A.2 GATE PARTICIPATION MEASUREMENT Unless fixed timestep is stated, we evaluate the conditioning pathway on 101 evenly spaced timesteps in [0, 1], including both endpoints, and all 1,000 ImageNet class labels. For each MLP gate vector α(t, y) RD, we compute nPR(α) = ((cid:80) d) and take the arithmetic mean over the 101,000 conditions, which gives nPR(α). We average participation values rather than gate vectors, and do not concatenate MHSA and MLP gates. Gates are computed in FP32 and statistics in FP64. We use the convention xt = (1 t)xdata + txnoise and convert it to each checkpoints input convention. In the scatter plots, regression lines are ordinary least-squares fits of FID to nPR(α), and is the Pearson correlation across the plotted runs. d)2/(D (cid:80) α2 α4 A.3 FID EVALUATION Local FIDs use the ADM evaluator (Dhariwal & Nichol, 2021) and the ImageNet-256 reference statistics, with 50,000 generated images, EMA model weights, the sd-vae-ft-ema decoder, CFG 1.5, and sampling seed 42. The sampler is adaptive DormandPrince (dopri5) (Dormand & Prince, 1980), with absolute tolerance 106 and relative tolerance 103. Besides FID (Heusel et al., 2017), the evaluator reports sFID (Dhariwal & Nichol, 2021), inception score (IS) (Salimans et al., 2016), and precision and recall (Kynkaanniemi et al., 2019). The gate intervention pilot and the teacher sweep use different protocols, described in Appendices B.2 and B.5.
